The real ambiguity has to come from conversation membership instead — I'm thinking about designing the query so the discriminating condition is which specific set of channels a reacting user belongs to (say, infra-related channels), so that the underspecification arises from at least two plausible candidate user sets tied to that shared membership pattern.

Given the seed data only has one reaction on record (U01AGENBOT9 reacting "eyes" to a message in the engineering channel), I think it makes more sense to invent a fresh scenario with multiple users reacting with an emoji like 🎉 to different messages, so I can build the identifying path backward: workspace → conversation → membership → user → reaction → message.

I'm thinking about using name ambiguity as the underspecified element — there are two distinct people named Robert (Robert Walsh and Robert Chen) who belong to different sets of channels, so referencing "Robert" without a surname could plausibly point to either one unless the reaction and channel context narrows it down.

So I'll set up separate reaction events: Robert Walsh reacting with 🎉 to an engineering message in C03IJKL9012, and Robert Chen reacting with 🎉 to a different message in C_INFRA, creating two distinct plausible referents depending on which Robert is meant.

For negatives, I'll include Robert Walsh reacting with 👍 instead of 🎉 on another message (so it doesn't count), plus a different non-Robert user reacting with 🎉 to yet another message, to make sure the emoji-plus-name combination stays the distinguishing factor.

Now I'm laying out the roles: two candidate messages (one in engineering reacted to by Robert Walsh, one in infra reacted to by Robert Chen) as matches/alternatives, their respective users, channel memberships, channels, workspace, and the corresponding reaction records as supporting/matching roles.

I also need negative distractors — Robert Walsh reacting with thumbsup elsewhere, and a different (non-Robert) user reacting with 🎉 elsewhere — to keep things distinct. The prompt itself can just be a natural, single-sentence request: asking to pull up the text of the message Robert reacted to with a 🎉, without hinting at any ambiguity. Then the binding note explains that ambiguity arises because two separate users named Robert (Walsh in engineering, Chen in infra) each reacted with 🎉 to different messages, creating two valid referent sets — so this is an underspecified case with candidates.

Now I'm drafting the two candidate messages and their reaction records with consistent IDs, timestamps, and channel/user fields to match the schema.

I'll add a 'tada' reaction from Robert on each candidate message, plus a separate 'thumbsup' reaction from Robert on an unrelated message to serve as a negative/distractor case.

I also want a genuine negative distinguishing example: someone else, like U_LUKAS, reacting with 'tada' on a message from U_SOPHIE that's unrelated to Robert, so the same emoji appears but tied to a different reactor entirely.

Checking membership, both U03ROBERT23 and U_ROBERT already have their channel memberships established in the seed data, so I don't need to add anything there — just the new messages and reactions. Now I'm working out the access plan, describing how someone could discover these reactions through conversation history or reaction lookups rather than a direct search for the emoji itself.

So my plan is to pull channel lists, fetch message histories, check reactions.get on each message for 🎉, then cross-reference the reactors via users.info to find candidates named "Robert." Now I'll put together the final JSON.
